nuggets.title: 9GB Upload Restart Forces Full Retry From Zero

scenario.symptoms: Users report failed 10GB video uploads after brief Wi-Fi drops; mobile clients restart entire uploads from byte zero.
scenario.interviewerSetup: Upload API accepts only single-shot multipart posts with no resumable session tokens or committed part manifests.

incident.headline: Non-resumable upload API wastes bandwidth after transient network loss

agenda.goal: Design a mechanism to reliably upload multi-gigabyte files that can resume after drops.
agenda.opener: If a user is uploading a 10 GB file and their network drops at 9 GB, how does your system handle it?

evidence.strong: Splits files into blocks (e.g., 4MB), uploads in parallel, retries only failed blocks, and commits via a manifest.
evidence.adequate: Mentions chunking or multipart upload for resuming.
evidence.weak: Attempts to stream the whole file over one TCP connection with no resume capability.

misconceptions.pattern: If an upload fails, we just retry the whole file from the beginning.
misconceptions.challenge: What happens if a user on a flaky connection tries to upload a 5 GB file?

probes: How does the server know when all the parts have arrived?
What size would you make the chunks and why?
hints: Is there a way to split the file before it leaves the client?
Look into how S3 handles multipart uploads.
agenda.referenceFix: Used chunked, multipart uploads to allow resuming failed transfers.

nuggets.title: App Servers OOM During Viral File Drop

scenario.symptoms: API fleet memory saturates during a campus-wide file share event; upload throughput collapses despite auto-scaled pods.
scenario.interviewerSetup: All file bytes proxy through application servers before reaching object storage.

incident.headline: Proxy uploads through app tier exhaust memory under large file fan-in

agenda.goal: Offload large file data transfers from application servers to storage directly.
agenda.opener: How do you prevent your application servers from becoming a bottleneck during massive file uploads?

evidence.strong: Issues pre-signed URLs from the metadata service, allowing the client to PUT directly to object storage.
evidence.adequate: Mentions uploading to object storage directly but vague on the security mechanism.
evidence.weak: Routes multi-GB uploads through standard application servers, exhausting memory.

misconceptions.pattern: The frontend sends the file to the backend, which streams it to storage.
misconceptions.challenge: How much network bandwidth will your backend instances need if 1,000 users upload 1 GB files simultaneously?

probes: How do we ensure the user is authorized to write to that specific storage bucket location?
How does the metadata service know the direct upload succeeded?
hints: Can the client talk directly to the storage layer?
Most cloud providers offer temporary credentials or URLs for direct secure access.
agenda.referenceFix: Used pre-signed URLs for direct client-to-storage uploads.

nuggets.title: Edits on Laptop Invisible on Phone for 20 Minutes

scenario.symptoms: Cross-device sync delays spike; users see stale folder listings on secondary devices after edits on primary.
scenario.interviewerSetup: Change notifications rely on clients polling every 15 minutes instead of push/webhook fanout.

incident.headline: Polling-based sync misses real-time change propagation to peer devices

agenda.goal: Ensure devices quickly learn about changes made by other devices or users.
agenda.opener: When a file is updated on one device, how do a user's other devices find out about the change?

evidence.strong: Uses WebSockets or long polling connected to a pub/sub system to push invalidations or change events.
evidence.adequate: Mentions polling or push notifications to trigger a sync.
evidence.weak: Relies on naive polling every minute, burning client battery and server CPU.

misconceptions.pattern: The client fetches the whole file list from the server every time a sync happens.
misconceptions.challenge: If a user has 100,000 files and only one changed, how do we avoid transferring the whole list?

probes: How do we scale the connections if we have 10 million online devices?
What message queue or broker helps route the events to the right server?
hints: If a client wants to be notified immediately, what connection type should it use?
How does the server know which device is subscribed to which user's folders?
agenda.referenceFix: Designed a real-time notification service to trigger client syncs.

nuggets.title: Offline Edit Merge Produces Duplicate Conflicting Copies

scenario.symptoms: Support tickets spike for duplicate files named doc (conflict 1) after users edited the same note offline on two devices.
scenario.interviewerSetup: Sync merges by last-write-wins using server arrival time without operational transform or user resolution.

incident.headline: Naive LWW merge silently forks concurrent offline edits

agenda.goal: Resolve cases where a file is edited concurrently on different offline devices.
agenda.opener: What happens if a user edits the same file on their laptop and phone while both are offline, and then both reconnect?

evidence.strong: Uses version vectors or a server-side version counter to detect forks, creating a 'conflicted copy' for the user to resolve.
evidence.adequate: Recognizes the conflict and explicitly defaults to last-writer-wins with history.
evidence.weak: Overwrites data silently based on client wall-clock time.

misconceptions.pattern: We can use the client's timestamp to decide which edit is newer and discard the older one.
misconceptions.challenge: What if the user actually wanted both sets of changes, or the client's clock is out of sync?

probes: How does the server definitively know the file was edited concurrently and not sequentially?
How do you communicate the conflict back to the user?
hints: What does Dropbox do when you and a friend edit the same document?
Can the server track which version the client started editing from?
agenda.referenceFix: Handled conflicts gracefully by creating conflicted copies.

scenario.symptoms: Storage costs jump 40% after a meme circulates; each user upload creates a unique object key with full byte copy.
scenario.interviewerSetup: Deduplication is disabled; content addressing and chunk hashing are not used on ingest.

incident.headline: Missing content-hash dedupe multiplies storage for identical uploads

agenda.goal: Save storage costs by not storing identical file content twice.
agenda.opener: If ten thousand users all upload the exact same popular video, how could we optimize our storage costs?

evidence.strong: Computes a hash of chunks on the client, checking if the block exists on the server before uploading.
evidence.adequate: Hashes whole files to prevent storing duplicates.
evidence.weak: Suggests scanning file names to find duplicates.

misconceptions.pattern: Deduplicating files based on their filename and size.
misconceptions.challenge: What if two different users have completely different files that happen to both be named 'video.mp4'?

probes: How do we ensure privacy and security if one user can access a block uploaded by another?
When is the hash computed: on the client or the server?
hints: If we identify files by their content rather than their name, how would we do it?
Could the client ask the server 'do you already have this chunk' before sending it?
agenda.referenceFix: Applied chunk-level deduplication via content hashing to save storage.
